lessons.title: What the ♲ numbers mean
paragraphs: The small triangle with a number from 1 to 7 is the Resin Identification Code. It tells you which plastic an item is made of: 1 PET, 2 HDPE, 3 PVC, 4 LDPE, 5 PP, 6 PS and 7 'other'.
The code describes the material. It does not promise that the item will be recycled. The arrows look like the recycling symbol, which confuses many people.
When PlasticLens is unsure, the printed code is the best way to check. It is usually moulded into the base of bottles and tubs.

lessons.title: Clean, dry and loose
paragraphs: Food and liquid left in packaging can spoil a whole load of recycling. A quick rinse is usually enough; packaging does not need to be spotless.
Keep items loose rather than bagged unless your scheme asks for bags. Sorting machines cannot open bags, and plastic films tangle in the equipment.
Small items such as bottle tops and sachets often fall through screens at sorting centres. Check whether your scheme wants caps on the bottle or separate.

lessons.title: Reduce and reuse come first
paragraphs: Recycling saves material, but it still takes energy and transport. Plastic usually loses quality each time it is recycled.
Avoiding an item you do not need, or reusing one many times, saves more than recycling it once.
Easy swaps: a refillable bottle, a reusable shopping bag, a lunch box, and buying loose fruit and vegetables.

lessons.title: Where plastic goes
paragraphs: Plastic that escapes waste collection can travel through drains and rivers into the sea. Sunlight and waves break it into smaller and smaller pieces.
Pieces smaller than 5 mm are called microplastics. They have been found in seawater, soil and food chains.
Burning plastic in the open releases harmful smoke, and PVC releases chlorine compounds. Putting plastic into proper collection keeps it out of the environment.
